To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the transcriptomes of CD4⁻ and CD8⁻ cells of RPs were similar to those of SIV-infected pathogenic macaques, whereas the VNPs shared the transcriptome of the natural hosts; and 2) the expression of several genes, such as CASP1 and TNFSF13, correlated with disease progression in a cohort of HIV-1-infected individuals.

the transcriptome of viremic non-progressors (VNPs), a subset of HIV-infected individuals that maintains high CD4 T cell counts despite high viral loads, is similar to that of natural hosts of simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), which do not progress to disease.

we identified the gene expression signatures of rapid progressors and viremic controllers of HIV-1 infection in humans and nonpathogenic Sooty mangabeys and rhesus monkeys infected with SIV, respectively, and we showed that the gene expression profiles of rapid progressors are similar to those of rhesus monkeys with AIDS, while the viremic controller profiles resemble those of sooty mangabees.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel therapeutic interventions for HIV infection.
understanding the molecular basis of human HIV disease progression and the role of host genetics.
the study of HIV infection in humans and SIV infection of nonhuman primates, and the identification of host genes that may be relevant for the control of HIV/SIV infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the transcriptome of the CD4⁺ cells of VNPs is similar to that observed during the nonpathogenic infection of the sooty mangabees, whereas the RP cells have a transcriptome similar to that of the pathogenic infection of the rhesus macaquess.
the RP transcriptome is similar to pathogenic SIV infection, whereas the VNP transcriptome resembles the nonpathogenic SAV infection.
the VNPs and RPs are characterized by specific transcriptome profiles that are similar to those of SIV-infected nonprogressive and pathogenic hosts, respectively.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified a set of genes that may be associated with disease progression and that these genes may also be associated with disease in natural hosts.

the transcriptome profiles of RPs are more similar to those of rhesus macacques infected with SIV, whereas the transcriptome profiles for VNPs are more similar than those of sooty mangabeyses infected with SIV.
the transcriptional profiles in the CD4⁺ cells of VNPs are more similar to those of nonpathogenic SOTUs than to those of RP, while the profiles in RP CD4⁺ are similar to those of RMs.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the transcriptomes of RPs resemble the transcriptomes of rhesus macaquess, while VNPs resemble those of sooty mangabeyses, and that these transcriptomes can be used to predict the time to disease progression in HIV-1-infected individuals.
the transcriptome of viremic non-progressors is similar to the one of natural hosts of the simian immunodeficiency virus.

the transcriptional profile of VNPs is similar to that of SIV-infected natural hosts, which is in contrast to that of RPs, which more closely resembles that of SIV infected rhesus macaqes, a non-natural host.
